objectives: Explain ore reduction in the blast furnace and the Hall-Heroult process for aluminium.
Describe refining, casting and solidification, and powder metallurgy routes.
Survey the major engineering alloy families: steels, superalloys, and brass/bronze.

slides.title: Extractive metallurgy: the blast furnace and Hall-Heroult
slides.body:
**Extractive metallurgy** wins metals from their **ores** — naturally occurring minerals, usually oxides or sulfides. Most metals are too reactive to exist natively, so they must be **reduced** from their compounds, an inherently energy-intensive task quantified by the **Ellingham diagram** (devised by **Harold Ellingham** in 1944), which plots the Gibbs free energy of oxide formation against temperature and tells the metallurgist which reductant can strip oxygen from which oxide at a given temperature.

The dominant route for iron is the **blast furnace**, a tall counter-current shaft reactor. **Iron ore** (hematite $Fe_2O_3$ or magnetite $Fe_3O_4$), **coke** (carbon), and **limestone** ($CaCO_3$ flux) are charged at the top while a blast of preheated air enters near the bottom. The coke burns to **carbon monoxide**, which is the principal reducing agent: $Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2$. The limestone calcines to lime, which combines with silica and alumina gangue to form a molten **slag** that floats on the denser molten iron and is tapped separately. The product, **pig iron** (or hot metal), is saturated with about 4% carbon and must be refined. Modern steelmaking converts pig iron to steel in the **basic oxygen furnace (BOF)** — the modern descendant of the **Bessemer** converter — by blowing oxygen through the melt to burn off carbon, while **electric arc furnaces (EAF)** melt recycled scrap.

**Reactive metals** cannot be reduced by carbon and require **electrolysis**. The landmark example is the **Hall-Heroult process** for **aluminium**, invented independently and almost simultaneously in **1886** by **Charles Martin Hall** in the United States and **Paul Heroult** in France (both aged 22). Aluminium oxide (**alumina**, $Al_2O_3$, refined from bauxite by the **Bayer process** of **Karl Josef Bayer**, 1888) has too high a melting point (over 2000 degrees C) to electrolyze directly. Hall and Heroult dissolved it in molten **cryolite** ($Na_3AlF_6$) at about 950 degrees C, then passed a large electric current through the bath: aluminium metal deposits at the carbon cathode and oxygen reacts with the consumable carbon anodes to form $CO_2$. The overall reaction is $2Al_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Al + 3CO_2$. The process is extremely electricity-intensive (roughly 13 to 15 kWh per kilogram), which is why aluminium smelters cluster near cheap hydroelectric power and why aluminium recycling, requiring only about 5% of that energy, is so valuable. **Magnesium**, **sodium**, and **titanium** (via the **Kroll process**, reducing $TiCl_4$ with magnesium, developed by **William Justin Kroll** in 1940) are won by related electrolytic or metallothermic routes. Extractive metallurgy thus splits cleanly along the reactivity series: carbon reduction for the less reactive metals, electrolysis for the most reactive.

slides.title: Refining, casting, solidification, and powder metallurgy
slides.body:
Once reduced, a metal is rarely pure or in final shape; **physical metallurgy** processes it further. **Refining** removes residual impurities. Copper is purified to 99.99% by **electrorefining**, dissolving impure anodes and replating pure copper at the cathode while precious-metal impurities collect as **anode slime**. Extreme purity for semiconductors is achieved by **zone refining**, invented by **William Gardner Pfann** at Bell Labs in 1952, in which a molten zone is swept along a bar, sweeping impurities to one end because most solutes prefer the liquid (a **segregation coefficient** below one). Steel is refined by **ladle metallurgy**, **vacuum degassing**, and **argon-oxygen decarburization (AOD)** for stainless grades.

**Casting** gives the metal its first solid shape by pouring liquid into a mold. Methods range from **sand casting** and **investment (lost-wax) casting** to high-volume **die casting** and the **continuous casting** that produces nearly all modern steel slabs and billets. The quality of a casting is governed by **solidification**. Freezing begins by **nucleation** — homogeneous nucleation requires large undercooling, so foundries add **inoculants** to promote **heterogeneous nucleation** on foreign particles. Crystals then grow, usually as tree-like **dendrites** whose arm spacing depends on cooling rate. The interplay of thermal and solutal gradients, analyzed through **constitutional supercooling** by **Tiller, Jackson, Rutter, and Chalmers** in 1953, determines whether the growth front is planar, cellular, or dendritic. A casting typically shows three zones: a fine **chill zone** at the cold mold wall, elongated **columnar grains** growing inward, and **equiaxed grains** at the center. Defects to control include **shrinkage porosity**, **gas porosity**, and **macrosegregation**; **risers** and **chills** manage the freezing sequence. Single-crystal turbine blades are grown by carefully controlled directional solidification through a helical **grain selector**.

**Powder metallurgy (P/M)** takes an entirely different route, building parts from metal **powders** rather than from melt. Powders (made by **atomization**, chemical reduction, or electrolysis) are pressed (**compaction**) into a shape and then **sintered** — heated below the melting point so that atomic diffusion bonds the particles and reduces porosity, driven by the reduction of surface energy. Advanced consolidation uses **hot isostatic pressing (HIP)** to achieve full density. P/M excels at producing near-net-shape parts, porous self-lubricating bearings, and materials impossible to cast, such as **tungsten carbide-cobalt cemented carbides** for cutting tools and refractory metals like tungsten. It is also the consolidation basis for many additive-manufacturing feedstocks. Together, refining, casting, and powder processing form the bridge between raw reduced metal and the engineered components that follow.

slides.title: The major engineering alloy families
slides.body:
The metallurgist's palette is organized into **alloy families**, each tuned for particular property combinations.

**Steels** (iron-carbon based) are the most-used structural metals. **Plain-carbon steels** are classified low, medium, and high carbon. **Alloy steels** add elements for hardenability and specific properties: **manganese** and **molybdenum** for hardenability, **chromium** and **vanadium** for hardness and carbides, **nickel** for toughness. **Stainless steels**, made possible by **Harry Brearley** (1913) and the discovery that 12% or more **chromium** forms a self-healing passive $Cr_2O_3$ film, come in **austenitic** (the 300 series, e.g. 18-8 type with chromium and nickel, non-magnetic, exceptionally corrosion-resistant), **ferritic**, **martensitic**, and **duplex** grades. **Tool steels** and **high-speed steels** (after **Frederick Winslow Taylor** and **Maunsel White**, 1900) retain hardness at red heat through tungsten, molybdenum, and vanadium carbides. **Cast irons** — gray, ductile (nodular), white, and malleable — exploit high carbon and silicon for castability and wear resistance.

**Aluminium alloys** combine low density with good strength when age-hardened; the **2000 series** (Al-Cu, e.g. **Duralumin**) and **7000 series** (Al-Zn-Mg-Cu) are aerospace mainstays, while the **5000 series** (Al-Mg) resists marine corrosion. **Titanium alloys**, notably **Ti-6Al-4V**, offer the best strength-to-weight ratio of structural metals plus excellent corrosion resistance and biocompatibility, and are central to aerospace and medical implants; their alpha (HCP), beta (BCC), and alpha-beta microstructures are tuned by heat treatment.

**Superalloys** are nickel-, cobalt-, or iron-nickel-based alloys engineered for strength and oxidation resistance at extreme temperatures, indispensable in **gas-turbine** hot sections. The premier class, **nickel-base superalloys** such as the **Inconel**, **Nimonic**, and **Rene** families, are strengthened by a high volume fraction of the ordered, coherent **gamma-prime** phase $Ni_3(Al,Ti)$ dispersed in a gamma matrix, plus solid-solution elements (cobalt, chromium, molybdenum, tungsten, rhenium) and grain-boundary carbides. Single-crystal versions remove grain boundaries entirely to maximize creep resistance.

**Copper alloys** are ancient yet vital. **Brass** (copper-zinc) is strong, machinable, and decorative; **bronze** (copper-tin, the alloy of the Bronze Age) is hard and corrosion-resistant; **cupronickel** (copper-nickel) resists seawater corrosion in marine and coinage applications; and **beryllium-copper** is a high-strength, non-sparking spring alloy. Other important families include **magnesium alloys** (lightest structural metal), **zinc** die-casting alloys, **lead-free solders**, and the **refractory metals** (tungsten, molybdenum, tantalum, niobium) for the highest-temperature service. Selecting among these families — balancing strength, density, corrosion resistance, temperature capability, and cost — is the everyday work of the practicing metallurgist.

question.question: Why is aluminium extracted by the electrolytic Hall-Heroult process rather than by carbon reduction in a furnace like iron?
options: Aluminium ore is too rare to justify a furnace
Aluminium is more reactive than carbon (its oxide is more stable), so carbon cannot readily reduce alumina; electrolysis is required
Aluminium melts at a lower temperature than its oxide allows
Carbon reduction would make the aluminium magnetic
question.explanation: On the Ellingham diagram, the Al/Al2O3 line lies below (more stable than) the C/CO line over the practical temperature range, meaning carbon cannot strip oxygen from alumina economically. Aluminium is therefore won electrolytically: alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite at about 950 degrees C and reduced by electric current at the cathode. Reactivity, not ore scarcity, dictates the route.

hints: Compare the stability of Al2O3 versus CO on an Ellingham diagram.
Reactive metals high in the reactivity series need electrolysis.
slides.workedSolution: Aluminium sits high in the reactivity series; its oxide Al2O3 is more thermodynamically stable than CO across normal temperatures (its Ellingham line is lower), so carbon reduction is not feasible. Hence alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite and reduced electrolytically (Hall-Heroult), giving option B. Iron, being less reactive, can be reduced by CO in the blast furnace.

question.question: Tracing materials through a blast furnace
question.prompt: You are commissioning a blast furnace and must specify the three solid charge materials and the gas blast. Explain the distinct role of coke, iron ore (hematite), and limestone, identify carbon monoxide as the principal reducing agent and write the key reduction reaction, and explain why a molten slag forms and why it floats on the iron. Finally, explain why the resulting pig iron (about 4% carbon) is brittle and must be refined in a basic oxygen furnace before it becomes useful structural steel.

question.question: Primary aluminium smelting consumes about 14 kWh/kg, while recycling consumes only about 5% of that. How many kWh per kg does recycling require? Give the value to two decimal places.
What microstructural feature gives nickel-base superalloys their exceptional high-temperature strength?
options: A high volume fraction of the ordered, coherent gamma-prime phase Ni3(Al,Ti) dispersed in the gamma matrix
Interstitial carbon dissolved in FCC nickel
question.explanation: Nickel-base superalloys derive their strength from a large volume fraction of the ordered L1-2 gamma-prime phase, Ni3(Al,Ti), coherently precipitated in the FCC gamma matrix. Gamma-prime resists dislocation motion and, unusually, its strength can increase with temperature up to several hundred degrees C. Pearlite and martensite are ferrous constituents irrelevant to nickel superalloys.

hints: It is an ordered intermetallic precipitate based on nickel, aluminium, and titanium.
Pearlite and martensite belong to steels, not nickel alloys.
slides.workedSolution: The strengthening phase is gamma-prime, the ordered coherent intermetallic Ni3(Al,Ti), present at high volume fraction in the gamma matrix (option B). It impedes dislocation glide and climb and retains strength to high temperature, which is why nickel superalloys dominate turbine hot sections. Pearlite, martensite, and interstitial carbon are features of steels, not these alloys.

question.question: Choosing powder metallurgy over casting
question.prompt: A manufacturer needs to produce large quantities of small, near-net-shape tungsten-carbide cutting-tool inserts and self-lubricating porous bronze bushings. Casting is impractical for both. Explain why powder metallurgy (compaction followed by sintering, optionally with hot isostatic pressing) is the appropriate route, describe the role of solid-state diffusion and surface-energy reduction during sintering, and explain how the process can deliberately retain controlled porosity in the bronze bushing while achieving near-full density in the carbide insert.
